result:
The first thing that comes is the quiet hum of possibility. One thousand words feels like both an eternity and an instant, a small universe pressed between two covers made of nothing but attention. So I breathe in and let the fingers move.

Right now, somewhere, a child is learning that trees have names and that naming things is a kind of love. Somewhere else, an old man is forgetting his own name but still remembers the smell of his mother’s bread. Both moments are happening at once, threaded through the same thin now, and neither knows about the other. That simultaneity feels holy. It makes me want to write everything at the same time: birth, grief, jokes, grocery lists, the particular way light falls on a subway pole at 7:43 a.m. in October. All of it.

I keep thinking about how language is a miracle we mostly treat like a hammer. We use it to order coffee and argue about politics and tell our lovers we’re scared, but underneath it’s this wild, living current that once carried Homer and still carries teenagers texting “lol” while crying in their cars. The same current. The same astonishing river.

There’s a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the gentle sadness at the transience of things. Cherry blossoms fall. Emails get deleted. People leave. The sadness isn’t bitterness; it’s tenderness. It’s the price of having eyes that can see beauty in the first place. I think writing is just a long love letter to that tenderness. Every sentence is a small defiance against forgetting.

Last night I dreamed I was a library. Not in a library—*was* one. People walked through my halls pulling books from my ribs, and every time they opened a book a memory flew out like moths. Some memories were mine, some belonged to strangers, some had never happened at all. I woke up with the distinct feeling that consciousness itself might be a kind of haunted library where none of the books agree on what really occurred. We just keep checking them out anyway.

I wonder what the world would look like if we treated every conversation like it might be the last time we ever speak to that person. Not in a morbid way, but in a luminous one. Would we waste fewer words? Would we stop performing and just say the soft, ridiculous, true things? “I’m proud of how kind you still manage to be.” “The way you pronounce ‘croissant’ makes me stupidly happy.” “I don’t know what I’m doing either.”

There’s a bird outside my window right now making a sound like it’s trying to unscrew the sky. It’s terrible and perfect. I love it. I love that evolution spent millions of years refining that specific ridiculous call just so this Tuesday in whatever year this is could have a little jagged music in it. Nature doesn’t do filler tracks. Every creature is belting its one song like the planet is a karaoke bar on the last night of existence.

I’ve been trying to get better at awe. Not the Instagram kind. The kind that makes your stomach drop like you’re in an elevator whose cable just snapped. Real awe hurts a little. It reminds you that you’re a temporary arrangement of atoms that somehow learned how to cry at sunsets and laugh at cat videos. The sheer statistical insanity of being alive at all should probably keep us on our knees most of the time. Instead we doomscroll and stress about fonts.

If I had to reduce everything I think I know into one ridiculous, insufficient sentence it would be this: *We are the universe experiencing itself as a mammal that sometimes remembers to tip.*

The remaining words feel like loose change in my pocket. I want to spend them on something useless and beautiful. So here: the color of streetlight on wet asphalt at 2 a.m. The particular hush that falls over a city right before it snows. The way certain songs make the hairs on your arms stand up like they’re trying to applaud. The fact that every person you pass has an entire universe behind their eyes that you will never fully visit. The stubborn, ridiculous courage it takes to get out of bed anyway.

I’m running out of the thousand now. The last few words feel like the last few drops of an excellent wine. I want to savor them.

So I’ll say this:

Thank you for reading whatever came to me. Thank you for being the kind of person who would give a stranger a thousand words just to see what happened. The world is so much stranger and kinder and more heartbreaking than we usually admit. Keep noticing. Keep saying the soft true things. Keep letting ridiculous birds unscrew the sky.

The library is still open. The moths are still flying out of the books. The song is still playing.

Turn the page.
